script: University rankings are criticised for measuring the wrong things, and the criticism is fair but incomplete. The deeper problem is that they measure things that move slowly. Research output, reputation surveys and staff ratios all change over years, so a ranking published annually is mostly a copy of last year's ranking. Readers treat a change of two places as news when it is closer to noise, and universities respond to that reading rather than to the underlying figure. What would be more useful is a ranking that reported only what had changed by more than its own measurement error, and left everything else blank. That would look empty, which is why no publisher will produce one. A blank space sells nothing, and an ordered list of two hundred institutions sells a great deal, whether or not the order carries information. The demand is not for accuracy but for a list, and the publishers are supplying exactly what is asked for.

items.stem: What is the writer's main objection?
options: The data are out of date
items.rationale: The deeper problem identified is that the things measured change over years, so each ranking largely copies the last.

items.stem: How do readers misread small changes?
items.rationale: A change of two places is treated as news when it is closer to noise.

items.stem: What would the writer's alternative look like?
items.rationale: Reporting only changes larger than the measurement error would leave most of the table blank.

items.stem: Why will no publisher produce it?
options: A blank table does not sell
items.rationale: The passage says a blank space sells nothing while an ordered list sells a great deal.

items.stem: What does the writer conclude about demand?
options: Readers want a list, not accuracy
items.rationale: The demand is for a list rather than accuracy, and publishers supply what is asked for.

script: It is often said that people no longer read books, and the evidence usually offered is a survey in which respondents report how many they finished last year. That evidence is weak for a reason that has nothing to do with honesty. Finishing is a poor unit. A reader who works through half of four difficult books has done more reading than one who finishes six light ones, and reports two thirds less. The unit persists because it is easy to count, and because publishing has an interest in counting sales rather than pages. Where reading time has been measured directly, by asking people to log what they did in a day, the picture is different: total time spent reading extended prose has fallen much less than book counts suggest, and a large share of it has moved to screens. Whether that move matters is a separate argument, and a real one. What is not real is the collapse the surveys describe, which is partly an artefact of asking a question whose answer is easy to give.

items.stem: Why is finishing a poor unit?
items.rationale: A reader who half-finishes four difficult books has read more but reports far less.

items.stem: Why does the unit persist?
items.rationale: It persists because it is easy to count and publishing counts sales.

items.stem: What do time-log studies show?
items.rationale: Total time reading extended prose has fallen much less than book counts suggest.

items.stem: Where has much reading moved?
items.rationale: A large share of the reading time has moved to screens.

items.stem: What does the writer accept is arguable?
options: Whether the move to screens matters
items.rationale: The writer calls the significance of the move to screens a separate and real argument.

script: Every few years a company announces that it has removed job titles, and the announcement is received as a move towards equality. It rarely is. A title is a public statement of where someone sits, and removing it does not remove the hierarchy; it removes the evidence. In an organisation without titles, seniority is still real, but it is now inferred from who speaks first in meetings, who is copied into which messages, and who has been there longest. Those signals are available to people who already understand the culture and invisible to newcomers, which is the opposite of what the change was meant to achieve. There is a stronger version of the reform, and it is much less popular. It keeps the titles and publishes the criteria for each one, so that a person can see what would have to be true for them to hold the next title. That is uncomfortable, because the criteria have to be written down and defended, and because a published criterion can be shown to have been applied inconsistently. Removing titles requires no such exposure, which is a reasonable explanation of why it is the version companies choose.

items.stem: What does removing titles actually remove?
items.rationale: The hierarchy remains real; what goes is the public evidence of where people sit.

items.stem: Who is disadvantaged by the change?
items.rationale: The remaining signals are visible to those who know the culture and invisible to newcomers.

items.stem: What is the stronger reform?
items.rationale: The stronger version keeps titles and publishes the criteria for each.

items.stem: Why is that version uncomfortable?
items.rationale: A published criterion can be shown to have been applied inconsistently, which requires exposure.

items.stem: How does the writer explain the popular choice?
items.rationale: Removing titles requires no exposure, which the writer offers as the explanation.

script: A common argument against paying research participants is that money attracts people who will say whatever they are asked to say. The concern is reasonable and the conclusion drawn from it is not. Unpaid participation does not remove the bias; it selects a different one. The people who volunteer for nothing are those with time, interest in the subject, and often a view about it already, which is a worse starting point for most questions than a group assembled by payment. What payment does introduce is a duty to design the study so that saying the expected thing is not the easy path, and that duty exists whether or not anyone is paid. The practical position is therefore the reverse of the usual one. Pay, because it widens the pool towards people who would not otherwise appear, and spend the effort on the instrument rather than on the recruitment. The studies that have compared paid and unpaid samples on the same questions find the paid samples closer to the population on demographics and no worse on response quality, which is the comparison the objection has always needed and rarely cites.

items.stem: What does unpaid participation do?
items.rationale: Unpaid participation does not remove bias; it selects a different one.

items.stem: Who volunteers for nothing?
items.rationale: Those with time, interest and often a prior view are the ones who volunteer unpaid.

items.stem: What duty does the writer say always exists?
items.rationale: The duty to design so that saying the expected thing is not easy exists whether or not anyone is paid.

items.stem: What does the writer recommend?
items.rationale: The practical position is to pay, widening the pool, and spend effort on the instrument.

items.stem: What do comparison studies find?
options: Paid samples match the population better
items.rationale: Paid samples are closer to the population on demographics and no worse on response quality.

script: The proposal to replace written examinations with continuous assessment is usually defended on the ground that examinations measure performance under artificial pressure, and it is true that they do. What the defence does not address is that continuous assessment measures something else artificial, namely the conditions under which the student happened to be living during the term. A student with a quiet room and no paid work produces better coursework than one without, and the difference is invisible in the mark. An examination compresses the inequality into three hours; coursework spreads it across twelve weeks. Neither removes it, and there is no reason to assume that the shorter exposure is the more distorting one. There is evidence on this, and it does not support the confident version of either position. Where institutions have moved from one system to the other, the gap between students from different backgrounds has generally narrowed slightly for coursework in subjects with clear right answers and widened for coursework in subjects where the mark rewards presentation and reading beyond the syllabus. That pattern is consistent with a plain reading: coursework rewards resources, and how much depends on how much the subject lets resources show. The honest conclusion is not that one should be preferred but that the choice is subject-specific, and that a faculty adopting a single policy across every department has decided the question without asking it. There is a further complication that neither camp raises, because it is inconvenient to both. A student who knows the assessment is continuous adjusts their whole term to it, and a student who knows it is a single examination adjusts theirs differently, so the two systems are not measuring the same students under different conditions. They are measuring students who have organised twelve weeks around different incentives, and no comparison of marks can separate the instrument from the behaviour it produced.

items.stem: What does the writer say about examinations?
items.rationale: An examination compresses the inequality into three hours while coursework spreads it across twelve weeks.

items.stem: What does coursework additionally measure?
items.rationale: Coursework measures the conditions under which the student happened to be living during the term.

items.stem: What does the evidence show?
options: The effect depends on the subject
items.rationale: Gaps narrowed for subjects with clear right answers and widened where marks reward presentation and outside reading.

items.stem: What reading is consistent with that pattern?
items.rationale: The passage says the pattern fits coursework rewarding resources to the degree the subject lets them show.

items.stem: What does the writer say about a single faculty policy?
items.rationale: A faculty adopting one policy across every department has decided the question without asking it.

script: Museums that have begun returning objects to the countries they were taken from are frequently warned that they are opening a door that cannot be closed, and the warning is usually presented as though it settled the matter. It does not, because it is an argument about consequences and consequences can be examined. The countries that have made the largest number of requests have made a few dozen each, not thousands, and they have concentrated on objects whose removal is documented and contested rather than on the general contents of a collection. Where returns have happened, the receiving institutions have in most cases lent the objects back for exhibition, sometimes within a year. The door, in other words, has been opened repeatedly and has not produced the emptying that was predicted. There is a serious version of the objection and it is not about volume. It is that a museum which returns an object on the basis of how it was acquired has adopted a principle it cannot apply evenly, because the acquisition history of most objects in most collections is simply unknown, and a principle applied only where the record happens to survive rewards institutions that kept poor records. That is a real difficulty. It is also an argument for reconstructing the records rather than for declining to act on the ones that exist, which is what it is usually used to support. A last point concerns who is doing the warning. It is almost never the curators who handle the requests, who describe a process that is slow, documented and case by case, and almost always commentators at some distance from it. That is not in itself an argument, since distance sometimes clarifies. But a prediction of collapse made repeatedly for twenty years, by people not involved in the transactions that were supposed to cause it, has accumulated a record, and the record is available to anyone who wants to weigh the prediction rather than repeat it.

items.stem: How does the writer treat the warning?
options: As a testable claim about consequences
items.rationale: The warning is an argument about consequences and consequences can be examined.

items.stem: What do the requests actually look like?
items.rationale: Countries have made a few dozen requests each, concentrated on documented and contested removals.

items.stem: What often happens after a return?
options: The object is never seen again
items.rationale: Receiving institutions have in most cases lent the objects back for exhibition.

items.stem: What is the serious version of the objection?
options: The principle cannot be applied evenly
items.rationale: Most acquisition histories are unknown, so the principle can only be applied where records survive.

items.stem: What does the writer say that difficulty supports?
items.rationale: It is an argument for reconstructing records rather than for declining to act on those that exist.

script: There is a standing argument that scientific papers should be shorter, and it is made almost entirely by people who read them rather than by people who write them. The reading case is easy: a paper that takes an hour to extract one finding from has wasted most of that hour, and a field publishing forty thousand papers a year cannot be read at that rate by anyone. The writing case is rarely stated and is stronger than it looks. Length in a modern paper is mostly method, and method is what allows a reader to judge whether the finding survives the way it was obtained. A short paper is not a paper with less padding; it is usually a paper in which the choices that could have gone another way have been moved into a supplement that nobody reads or omitted entirely. The replication difficulties of the last decade have fallen disproportionately on fields whose conventions favour short reports, and the direction of that association is at least suggestive. The reform that follows is not shorter papers but differently shaped ones: a finding stated in a paragraph that a reader can evaluate for relevance, followed by the method at whatever length honesty requires, with nothing removed to meet a limit. Journals could do this tomorrow, and the reason most have not is that page limits are a convenient rationing device for editorial attention, which is a real constraint being solved at the reader's expense rather than a judgement about what a paper should contain.

items.stem: Who mainly argues for shorter papers?
items.rationale: The argument is made almost entirely by people who read papers rather than by those who write them.

items.stem: What does length in a modern paper mostly consist of?
items.rationale: The passage states that length is mostly method, which lets a reader judge how the finding was obtained.

items.stem: What is a short paper usually missing?
items.rationale: In a short paper such choices have been moved to an unread supplement or omitted.

items.stem: What does the writer note about replication problems?
options: They cluster where reports are short
items.rationale: Replication difficulties have fallen disproportionately on fields whose conventions favour short reports.

items.stem: Why do page limits persist?
items.rationale: Page limits are described as a convenient rationing device for editorial attention.

script: Cities that have introduced a tax on empty homes usually justify it as a housing measure, and judged as one it has performed poorly nearly everywhere it has been tried. The number of dwellings brought back into use has been small, typically well under two per cent of the stock the tax applies to, and the reason is not mysterious: an owner who can afford to leave a property empty in an expensive city can generally afford a tax calculated as a fraction of its value. What the measure has done, consistently and almost incidentally, is produce a register. To levy the tax at all a city must establish which properties are occupied, and doing so has repeatedly revealed that the estimates it was previously working from were wrong, sometimes by a factor of two in either direction. That is a substantial result and it is never the one claimed. There is an argument that a measure justified on one ground and delivering on another should be rejected as dishonest, and I think it is the wrong argument. The right one is that the register should be built directly, at a fraction of the cost and without the political expenditure a tax requires, and that cities keep choosing the tax because a register is not a policy anyone can campaign on. The cost of that preference is not the tax revenue. It is the years spent before anyone knows how many homes are actually empty. There is a version of the tax that answers this objection and it is not the one adopted anywhere. Levy it at a rate high enough to change the owner's arithmetic rather than at a rate calibrated to be politically survivable, and accept that the revenue will fall towards zero if it works, which is what a tax intended to change behaviour ought to do. No city has done this, and the reason is visible in every budget that counts the receipts as income.

items.stem: How has the tax performed as housing policy?
items.rationale: Judged as a housing measure it has performed poorly nearly everywhere, returning under two per cent to use.

items.stem: Why do owners absorb the tax?
options: They can afford the fraction charged
items.rationale: An owner able to leave a property empty can generally afford a tax that is a fraction of its value.

items.stem: What has the measure produced instead?
items.rationale: To levy the tax a city must establish which properties are occupied, producing a register.

items.stem: What did those registers reveal?
items.rationale: They revealed previous estimates were wrong, sometimes by a factor of two in either direction.

items.stem: What does the writer say cities should do?
items.rationale: The register should be built directly at a fraction of the cost, without the political expenditure a tax requires.

script: The claim that a national language policy can be neutral between its languages is one of those propositions that survives because nobody states it plainly enough to test. Stated plainly it says that a state can conduct its business in two languages without advantaging either, and the mechanism usually proposed is symmetry: everything published in one appears in the other, every official may be addressed in either, every form exists twice. Symmetry of provision is achievable and has been achieved in several places. What it does not produce is symmetry of use, because the two are connected by a variable that policy does not control. A speaker choosing which language to open a conversation in is making a prediction about the other person, and the safe prediction is the language more people know. Symmetrical provision leaves that prediction untouched, which is why bilingual institutions drift towards the majority language in their corridors while remaining scrupulously bilingual in their documents. The policies that have altered use rather than provision have all done something asymmetrical: reserved posts, a language of internal record, a requirement that meetings open in the minority language unless someone asks otherwise. Each of these is criticised as unfair on the symmetry principle, and each is defended by its supporters as a correction to an existing asymmetry rather than the creation of a new one. That defence is coherent, and it is also the point at which the neutrality claim has to be abandoned rather than refined, because a policy that corrects an imbalance is by construction not neutral between the parties to it. One further observation belongs here because it is where the argument usually stops. Every asymmetrical measure creates a class of people who are disadvantaged by it, and those people are real and their complaint is not manufactured. What the neutrality claim does is allow their complaint to be answered with an appeal to a principle rather than with an argument about which imbalance is larger, which is the argument that actually has to be won.

items.stem: What does symmetry of provision achieve?
items.rationale: Symmetry of provision is achievable but does not produce symmetry of use.

items.stem: What governs which language a speaker opens in?
items.rationale: A speaker is predicting what the other person knows, and the safe prediction is the more widely known language.

items.stem: What happens in bilingual institutions?
items.rationale: They drift towards the majority language in corridors while remaining bilingual in documents.

items.stem: What do effective policies have in common?
items.rationale: Policies that altered use have all done something asymmetrical, such as reserved posts or a language of record.

items.stem: What does the writer conclude about neutrality?
options: It must be abandoned, not refined
It can be achieved with effort
items.rationale: A policy that corrects an imbalance is by construction not neutral, so the claim has to be abandoned.

script: Peer review is defended on the ground that it catches error and attacked on the ground that it does not, and both sides tend to argue as though the question were empirical in a straightforward way. It is not, because what counts as catching error depends on a decision about what review is for that is rarely made explicitly. If the purpose is to certify that a finding is correct, then review fails obviously and often, and the studies in which deliberate errors are inserted into manuscripts and go unnoticed are the relevant evidence. If the purpose is to establish that a paper is competent, complete and worth the attention of a specialist audience, then those same studies are close to irrelevant, because a planted arithmetic error is not what an experienced reviewer is reading for. The second purpose is the one review actually serves, and it is the one nobody claims, because it is unimpressive: a filter that removes the plainly unready and leaves everything else to the field. Defending review honestly means defending that, and accepting what follows from it. A published paper is not certified. The reader's obligation does not end at the point of publication, and the practice of citing a claim on the strength of the journal it appeared in is not a shortcut but an error, one that the overselling of review has done a great deal to encourage. The reforms worth having follow from the modest description rather than the grand one, and most of them are about making the filter's decisions visible rather than about making the filter stronger. A last consideration concerns what would replace the overselling. Nothing dramatic is required, and the most useful change is also the least demanding: publishing the reports alongside the paper, so that a reader can see what was asked and what was answered. Where that has been done, it has not improved the reviews noticeably, and it has changed what readers do with them, which was always the more tractable half of the problem.

items.stem: Why is the dispute not straightforwardly empirical?
options: The purpose of review is undecided
items.rationale: What counts as catching error depends on a rarely explicit decision about what review is for.

items.stem: When are the planted-error studies relevant?
items.rationale: They are relevant if the purpose is certifying that a finding is correct, and close to irrelevant otherwise.

items.stem: Which purpose does the writer say review serves?
items.rationale: The second purpose, a filter removing the plainly unready, is the one review actually serves.

items.stem: Why is that purpose rarely claimed?
items.rationale: The passage calls it unimpressive, which is why nobody claims it.

items.stem: What error does overselling encourage?
items.rationale: Citing a claim on the strength of the journal it appeared in is called an error the overselling encourages.

script: Arguments about whether a technology destroys jobs are conducted almost entirely at the wrong level of aggregation. At the level of the economy the historical answer is settled and uninteresting: employment has not fallen across two centuries of mechanisation, and anyone predicting that it will this time is making a claim that has been wrong every previous time it was made. At the level of the individual the answer is equally settled and points the other way: a person whose occupation disappears in their fifties does not, on the evidence, move into the new occupations the same technology creates. They move into lower-paid work in the same region or they leave the labour force. Both statements are true, and the argument persists because each side treats its own level as the real one. What follows is not a compromise but a redirection. If aggregate employment is not the thing at risk, then policies defending it — subsidies to keep an industry alive, restrictions on adoption — are addressing a problem that will not occur, at the cost of the productivity gain that is the entire point. If individual displacement is the thing at risk, then the instruments that address it are income support, portable benefits, and regional investment, none of which requires slowing the technology at all. The two propositions are not in tension; the policy conclusions drawn from them have simply been assigned to the wrong one. A country that protects the industry and neglects the worker has managed to pay for both errors at once, and that combination is more common than either error alone. There is a timing point that neither level captures, and it belongs to whoever has to act. The aggregate adjustment happens over a generation and the individual displacement happens in a quarter, so a policy that is right about the destination can still be wrong about every year on the way to it. That mismatch, rather than any disagreement about the eventual outcome, is what most political argument about technology is actually about.

items.stem: What is settled at the economy level?
items.rationale: Across two centuries of mechanisation employment has not fallen, which the writer calls settled and uninteresting.

items.stem: What happens to displaced older workers?
items.rationale: They move into lower-paid work in the same region or leave the labour force.

items.stem: Why does the argument persist?
options: Each side prefers its own level
items.rationale: The argument persists because each side treats its own level of aggregation as the real one.

items.stem: What does the writer say about protecting industries?
options: It solves a problem that will not arise
It is by far the cheapest option
It helps the displaced workers most
It slows adoption in a useful way
items.rationale: Defending aggregate employment addresses a problem that will not occur, at the cost of the productivity gain.

items.stem: What is the most common policy failure?
items.rationale: A country that protects the industry and neglects the worker pays for both errors, and that combination is most common.

script: The idea that a city should be planned so that daily needs lie within a short walk has acquired both enthusiastic supporters and a peculiar species of opponent, and the interesting failure belongs to neither. Supporters present the proximity as the mechanism, and it is not. What produces the effect they want is not distance but the density of destinations that distance implies, and the distinction matters because the two can be separated. A suburb can be rebuilt so that a shop lies four hundred metres from every house and still fail entirely, if the shop is the only destination and everyone drives past it to somewhere with choice. Proximity without variety produces a short walk nobody takes. The evidence from the districts held up as successes supports the second reading rather than the first: what they share is not a radius but a count, several dozen distinct destination types within the area, and the ones that failed had the radius without the count. This has an awkward implication for the policy, because a radius can be mandated and a count cannot. A planning authority can require a shop in a development and cannot require that thirty different kinds of business find it worth their while to be there, and the instruments that influence the second — permissive zoning, small premises, tolerance of change of use — are slower, less visible and much harder to announce. The version of the idea that gets adopted is therefore reliably the version that does not work, and its failure is then read as evidence against the idea rather than against the substitution. The failure has a further consequence that is rarely traced. Each unsuccessful development supplies a photograph of an empty parade of shops, and those photographs circulate as evidence about walkable neighbourhoods in general, without any accompanying account of how many destination types the development contained. A policy failure and an idea's refutation look identical in a photograph, which is one reason the substitution keeps being made.

items.stem: What do supporters wrongly identify as the mechanism?
items.rationale: Supporters present proximity as the mechanism, but the writer says the density of destinations is what produces the effect.

items.stem: Why can a nearby shop still fail?
items.rationale: Proximity without variety produces a short walk nobody takes, since people drive past to somewhere with choice.

items.stem: What do the successful districts share?
items.rationale: What they share is not a radius but several dozen distinct destination types within the area.

items.stem: Why is that awkward for policy?
items.rationale: A radius can be mandated and a count cannot, since businesses cannot be required to find a location worthwhile.

items.stem: What happens when the wrong version fails?
items.rationale: Its failure is read as evidence against the idea rather than against the substitution.
